references.text: Jesus pronounces a woe upon the Pharisees and compares them to unmarked graves. The parallel passage is found in Matt 23:27-28, where Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees "whitewashed tombs" that look beautiful on the outside but are full of dead men's bones and impurity inside.

The background for Jesus' image is the law concerning ritual uncleanness from contact with a dead body. In Num 19:16 it is stated that anyone who touches a dead person, a human bone, or a grave in an open field becomes unclean for seven days. The Pharisees are like hidden graves that make people unclean without their knowing it.
In Num 19:11 it is established that whoever touches a corpse becomes unclean for seven days. Jesus' point is that the Pharisees hide their uncleanness and thus defile others without them noticing.

The image of outward piety hiding inner corruption recalls Ps 5:10, where it says about the wicked that "their inmost being is destruction" and that "their throat is an open grave." Paul quotes this in Rom 3:13.

In Rom 3:13 Paul quotes Psalm 5:10 and says: "Their throat is an open grave." The image of the tomb as a symbol of spiritual corruption and uncleanness connects to Jesus' warning about the hidden uncleanness of the Pharisees.

The woe in verse 44 is part of a series of woes against the Pharisees that begins in Luke 11:42-43, where Jesus rebukes them for tithing herbs while neglecting justice and love for God, and for loving the places of honor.

The image of graves is used prophetically in Ezek 37:12-13, where God promises to open the graves and bring His people out. The contrast with Luke 11:44 is clear: while God opens graves and gives life, the hidden graves of the Pharisees are a source of uncleanness and spiritual death.
In Matt 23:25-26 Jesus uses a similar image about cleaning the outside of the cup while the inside is full of greed and self-indulgence—the same theme of outward purity covering inner impurity.
